newsitem.title: UK: European PC sales growth slows in 1996.
newsitem.headline: European PC sales growth slows in 1996.

text.p: Sales of personal computers in Europe lost momentum in 1996, pulled back by stodgy German sales and by customers waiting for the new MMX technology, according to a survey published Monday.

Western Europe's PC sales rose a healthy 11.5 percent in 1996 to 16.4 million, market researcher Context said. That compared with 25 percent sales growth in 1995 and projections of up to 15 percent made by analysts up until the end of August.
Compaq Computer S. retained its position as market leader.
Personal computer sales in 1997 may show some improvement.

"We're unlikely to see 1995 growth rates this year. Back then we saw 25 percent growth fuelled by a 30 percent rise in the consumer PC business," said Emmanuel Lalloz, senior PC research analyst at Context.

"However, there are signs that the market could pick up in the second half of this year as fourth-quarter 1996 growth was restrained as customers waited for Intel's Pentium MMX-powered machines to become more generally available," Lalloz said.

The effects of economic recession put a lid on sales, while in Spain and France, governments focusing on meeting the Maastricht criteria for economic and monetary union slashed spending on information technology, Context said.

Britain was the best market in Europe, with sales bounding 19.5 percent to 3.4 million. French sales grew 14.2 percent to 2.4 million, and in Germany, the biggest market in western Europe, sales rose a paltry 7.5 percent to 3.8 million.
Compaq, with sales of more than two million, saw its market leadership pared to 12.4 percent compared with 12.7 percent in 1995.
In second place, International Business Machines Corp. raised its market share to 9.7 percent from 9.2. percent.
Fujitsu Ltd, in eighth place with its ICL and Aquarius brands, scored the biggest gain in the top 10 with a 49.2 percent increase.
"Fujitsu targeted the fast-growing small-to-medium business segment with very aggressive pricing. Fujitsu also made a significant breakthrough in the corporate sector," Lalloz said.
Context said direct sellers continued to set the pace, with Dell Computer Corp. jumping one place to seventh.
Apple Computer lost 1.7 points of market share.

"Results for Apple however showed clear signs of recovery, with revenue jumping 50 percent in the fourth over the third quarter. Apple has now focused its strategy on the profitability issue, rather than volume, and has consequently decided to withdraw from the lowest price brands where the biggest volumes are," Lalloz said.
The biggest selling European brand was Siemens Nixdorf, in fifth place, followed by Olivetti, in ninth. Last month Olivetti sold its money-losing PC subsidiary.

The long-term prospects for Europe's PC sales are healthy, according to Lalloz. "The potential of western European markets remains enormous since the penetration rate of PCs in the home is still far lower than in the U.S.," he said.
About 35 percent of American homes have PCs, while barely 20 percent in Europe have them.
